items.body: Debbie Critchfield wants $20 million to help school districts and charters keep pace with inflation, and support at-risk students. Even if the 2027 Legislature signs on, the $20 million would get carved up quickly. But the state superintendent said she prefers to enter the next session with a workable request, and not one that is immediately dismissed as “ridiculous.” “I’d rather ask for something that I believe we can get to,” Critchfield said Wednesday. State Superintendent of Public Instruction Debbie Critchfield, a Republican running for another term in November, speaks to an attendee after a candidate forum on Tuesday, Aug. 4, 20206, in Boise. (Sean Dolan/EdNews) " data-large-file="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/IMG_0932-4-e1789069506928-1180x682.jpg" class="wp-image-123622 size-large" src="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/IMG_0932-4-1180x943.jpg" alt="" width="1180" height="943" /> State Superintendent of Public Instruction Debbie Critchfield, a Republican running for another term in November, speaks to an attendee after a candidate forum on Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, in Boise. (Sean Dolan/EdNews) In an EdNews interview, Critchfield discussed the 2027-28 spending request she submitted a week ago — and the political calculus that went into her budget. All told, Critchfield is seeking more than $3.3 billion for K-12, a 3.9% increase. But her one new budget request is a $20 million slice of the pie. She wants this increase to go into “operational” spending — commonly called discretionary funds, because districts and charters can use this line item for any purpose. And that makes it a popular request in the K-12 community, Critchfield said Wednesday. So far, she said, she has heard only positive feedback from school administrators. “(It’s) the most flexible and customizable part of the budget for districts and charters.” However, there also would be a lot of pressure on the $20 million. Operational funding, now at $366 million, has essentially been frozen for three years. An increase could help address inflation. Schools could also use the increase to cover unexpected bills from the Idaho School Benefit Trust. Districts and charters are on the hook for much of the trust’s $13 million shortfall — and as EdNews reported this week, employee medical claims could be denied if a member of the trust refuses to pay their share of the $13 million. The trust shortfall came to light in July, but Critchfield’s budget has no money to address it directly. Lastly, the new operational money could support a rewrite of Idaho’s aging school funding formula. Idaho politicians have long discussed changes to the formula, adopted in 1994. Supporters of a rewrite, including Critchfield, want to provide extra funding to support at-risk students, such as special education students. While $20 million won’t cover a new formula entirely, it could provide first-year funding, Critchfield said Wednesday. Dedicated dollars could smooth the transition, covering schools that would lose money under a new formula. And this would be a departure from 2025, when lawmakers debated a funding formula bill that had no dollars attached to it. While Critchfield is pushing the $20 million line item, the Republican is seeking less money for the special education program she navigated through the 2026 Legislature. Her budget contains $1.7 million for a “high-needs” fund, for students who require full-time staff support or costly equipment. This year’s high-needs budget is $5 million. items.body: University of Idaho President Scott Green presides over the 2022 commencement ceremony at the school's Moscow campus. (Photo courtesy of the University of Idaho) This story was originally posted on IdahoEdNews.org on Sept. 9, 2026. University of Idaho President C. Scott Green will retire on June 30. Green made the announcement during the president’s “state of the university” address Wednesday — an annual event that took a sudden and emotional turn. Addressing the campus community at his alma mater, Green recounted success stories from his seven-year tenure, including advances in enrollment, research and athletics. He also reflected on the challenges of leading the U of I through a global pandemic and in the aftermath of the November 2022 off-campus murders of four students. Flowers and candles left for a makeshift memorial sit near police tape at the site of a quadruple murder of four University of Idaho students on Jan. 3, 2023, in Moscow, Idaho. (Photo by David Ryder/Getty Images) “We truly were at our best when the Vandal family and the Moscow community needed us,” said Green, fighting back tears. “We love you, Scott,” one member of the audience said aloud, before the room rose in a standing ovation. Green’s departure marks a transition at the state’s land-grant university, and sets the stage for another top-tier job search. The State Board of Education — which doubles as the U of I’s Board of Regents — recently filled the president’s vacancy at Boise State University, after a tumultuous and largely closed-door 16-month search. ‘We accomplished more than most thought possible’ A former U of I student body president, Green returned to Moscow in July 2019 , leaving New York City and a top management position with Hogan Lovells, an international law firm. Green said he came back, in part, to bring some stability to the president’s office — a revolving door at the helm of a university established before Idaho’s statehood. During Wednesday’s speech, Green noted that his tenure marks the longest of any U of I president since Richard Gibb. Gibb was president while Green was a U of I undergrad. Green graduated in 1984. Green also discussed several milestones from his presidency. By spring 2020, the U of I had covered $40 million in operating losses , a shortfall inherited by Green. Enrollment rebounded from a pandemic-era lull. Last fall, the U of I welcomed its second-largest freshman class in history . In 2025, the U of I received top-tier R1 research status from the Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education , the first Idaho university to reach this threshold. Later that year, the U of I wrapped up a $500 million capital campaign . “We accomplished more than most thought possible,” Green said. On Wednesday, Green also revisited one of his signature initiatives, a failed bid to purchase the University of Phoenix, a massive for-profit online university with a national footprint and tarnished reputation. The State Board gave the Phoenix deal the green light in 2023, after a series of closed-door discussions. The 2024 Legislature balked at the bid — with some lawmakers grumbling that they had been cut out of the process. The U of I and Phoenix broke off negotiations in June 2025 . Green said the purchase — with an overall price tag of $685 million — would have landed Idaho an asset that has since gone on the public market for $1.1 billion . “History has already shown (this) was one of the greatest financial opportunities the state of Idaho will ever see,” Green said Wednesday. ‘He conquered that storm’ Green received plaudits Wednesday from top state leaders — including one of the state’s most prominent Vandal alums. “Scott Green has served the University of Idaho with dedication, integrity, and a deep commitment to the Vandal family,” Gov. The winner will also read their essay during the tree-lighting ceremony. Submissions must: Be between 350-500 words Be submitted by Sept. 30 Be an original essay written by the contest participant Certify the essay is not written by AI Have approval of a parent or guardian Submit essays here . items.body: The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho state government agencies’ budget requests for the next fiscal year are now publicly available. The requests, which are online on the Division of Financial Management’s website , are for Idaho’s fiscal year 2028, which starts July 1, 2027. After ‘tight budget year,’ Idaho ends fiscal year with positive cash balance On the heels of a 2026 Idaho legislative session marked by budget cuts after years of state tax cuts, the requests outline the state’s strategy of continuing to operate state agencies and public programs with less funding, according to the governor’s budget chief, Lori Wolff. In a media briefing last week, Wolff told reporters that non-discretionary funding for Medicaid, state prisons and public schools is eating up most of a recent projection of increased revenue. “We were very tight on our bottom line before, so it doesn’t give us a whole lot of room,” Wolff told reporters. “That really quickly takes up most of the increase in our revenue,” she said. “So, our focus this year is going to be on keeping those budgets at where we set them last year.” In May, she wrote a memo to state agencies instructing them to only submit barebones budgets, and that the next budget year was not the time to start restoring budget cuts . The budget request for the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare — the state’s largest government agency that runs Medicaid and other public assistance programs — is the only budget plan that hasn’t been published yet, the governor’s spokesperson, Emily Callihan, said in a statement. She said officials expect to post the agency’s budget request Tuesday. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE The requests are one of the first major steps in the process to fund state government. In January, Idaho Gov. Brad Little typically releases his own proposed state budget. Then the Idaho Legislature, which meets during the first few months of the calendar year, considers budget requests by state agencies and the governor as lawmakers draft budget bills. In recent years, Idaho’s powerful budget-setting committee, the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee, has shifted to a different budgeting process that splits agency budgets into barebones funding and new spending. items.body: A 2023 aerial shot of the Materials and Fuel Complex at the Idaho National Laboratory's desert site. The complex contains several specialized labs where INL researches nuclear fuels. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho National Laboratory) One of the most critical issues facing Idaho is one that has received little attention but has profound consequences for the future of our state – the agreement that would make Idaho the dumping ground for a third of the radioactive waste generated in our country. It’s not surprising that Idahoans don’t know much about this issue. Gov. Brad Little, who is pursuing this agreement , and U.S. Sen. Jim Risch have said precious little or nothing about it, apparently wanting to keep it under the radar until they are safely re-elected in November. New nuclear campus deal would require Idaho to accept, store spent nuclear fuel, radioactive waste Congressman Mike Simpson applauded the agreement , saying it will bring jobs to his eastern Idaho district. “Idaho didn’t become the nation’s nuclear leader by being afraid of hard problems. It became the leader by being the state willing to do the difficult, careful work that others wouldn’t. That’s still the right instinct now,” he wrote. The Trump administration will choose three states to create what it calls a “Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus.” The other states in the running for this dubious honor besides Idaho are Utah, Tennessee, Louisiana and Oklahoma. The chosen states will each have to receive 33 percent of the radioactive waste generated by the other 47 states. The public did not know that Gov. Little agreed to be one of the states until the Department of Energy announced it in late July. The memorandum of understanding that Little signed in July without informing Idahoans said: “The host agreement shall provide for the acceptance of out-of-state used nuclear fuel, spent fuel, and high-level radioactive waste.” In its announcement, the Trump administration promised that the campus will boost manufacturing, create jobs, promote American energy independence, and attract other unnamed financial investments. Of course, we don’t know what this means since Little and our congressional delegation have not told us what’s in the fine print. Idaho’s long history with nuclear waste To put the importance of this issue in perspective, it is important to understand Idaho’s long and dark history with radioactive waste. Starting in the 1940s, the federal energy site in eastern Idaho, which is now called the Idaho National Laboratory, became the repository for much of the nation’s nuclear radioactive waste. The issue came to a head in the late 1970s when the press reported that the federal facility had regularly poured low-level radioactive liquid waste down an injection well above the Snake River Aquifer, which is the size of Lake Erie and provides much of the water for southern Idaho’s farmers and ranchers. There was also concern about other radioactive liquid waste being stored in containers buried above the aquifer. I covered energy issues for t he Idaho Statesman at the time and reported on the controversy over this waste. There was concern among Idaho’s political leaders because the federal site was also known for its porous volcanic soil and seismic activity. Coverage of the issue made front page news for months. That same year the General Accounting Office recommended that Idaho become a permanent repository for the nation’s radioactive waste. That proposal came nine years after the federal government promised to remove the existing waste from Idaho. The GAO report was quickly opposed by then Gov. John Evans and even a Republican legislator from Boise who introduced a bill in the Legislature to ban any shipment of radioactive waste into our state. That’s despite Kuna’s rapid population growth, leaving the district with a disconnect between community growth and public school enrollment. Superintendent Marcus Myers laid out the district’s capacity and enrollment numbers in a presentation to trustees Tuesday night. Hubbard Elementary: 263 students in a building with a capacity of 400. Indian Creek Elementary: 238 students in a building with a capacity of 375. Fremont Middle School: 532 students in a building with a capacity of 750. Kuna Middle School: 726 students in a building with a capacity of 960. Enrollment has dropped by nearly 4% in the district since last school year, falling from 5,703 to 5,501. Yet in 2025, the U.S. Census Bureau named Kuna one of the fastest-growing cities in the nation. “Right now we do have some room, and we want our classrooms full for the sake of our kids and for the great opportunities that we afford to kids,” Myers told trustees. Some students are choosing alternatives to traditional public schools. About 2% of school-aged children within the district’s boundaries attend charters schools, Myers told Idaho Education News. Increasingly, parents have more options beyond traditional public schools. Valor Classical Academy, a charter school, opened its doors this year with around 450 students enrolled. Myers wants to have conversations with local families choosing charters to understand what influenced their decision. “It could have nothing to do with the Kuna School District,” he said. Myers told trustees he’s also working with the city to identify demographics of families moving into the area to learn how many have school-age children. He’s unsure when he will have the data. Kuna’s enrollment appears to reflect a statewide trend : Despite continued population growth across the state, overall K-12 enrollment is declining, particularly among elementary-age students. One factor is declining birth rates, which fell from over 16 per 1,000 residents in 2007 to under 12 per 1,000 residents in 2024, according to U.S. census data. Kuna has also seen its heaviest declines among elementary students. Some parents also cited homeschooling in a recent Kuna School District survey. Other families may be choosing private or charter schools, though it’s unclear how many students leaving public schools are taking advantage of Idaho’s $50 million Parental Choice Tax Credit. The Idaho State Tax Commission won’t release data showing how many recipients previously enrolled their children in public schools. The schools would use much of the money to bolster high-demand academic fields or cover the cost of growth. The budget request centers on a complicated line item that Gov. Brad Little refused to fund in 2026 — enrollment workload adjustment, or EWA. Using a three-year average of weighted credit hours, EWA is designed to provide additional money to growing colleges and universities. items.body: UPDATED 9/9/2026 with details about how the Assistance League uses its thrift shop revenue. Operation School Bell started in someone’s garage more than 30 years ago. Today, the volunteer program fills a warehouse with boxes of back-to-school supplies and new clothes for needy elementary students in Boise, Kuna and West Ada districts. The massive volunteer program begins with the Assistance League of Boise, which is funded by a small Garden City thrift store that generated $1 million last year, the most it’s ever made. It’s open Wednesday through Saturday for dropping off items or shopping for hand-picked, new-to-you treasures. Eighty percent of the store’s revenue goes toward funding Assistance League philanthropy efforts like Operation School Bell. This year, hundreds of students benefitted. “ I was raised by a single mom, so I would have benefited from these programs as a young student,” said Rebecca Kochvar, who has volunteered with the Assistance League of Boise since 2012. “It definitely feels like a real joy for me to be able to do this for students that would have been me in kindergarten through sixth grade.” Here’s how it works: Counselors and educators select students in need of clothes and supplies during the first days of school. These students are then transported in buses to the Assistance League of Boise’s “store,” a large room resembling the children’s clothing section of a department store, complete with racks of puffer coats, full-length mirrors and changing rooms. After choosing their new clothes, students get fitted for a new pair of shoes in another room. Volunteers — largely retired women — help kids find what fits. items.body: (BOISE) – Last year when I was pressed to identify cuts to our public schools, I declined. I knew schools couldn’t sustain mid-year cuts, let alone ongoing reductions. When I submit a K-12 public school budget, it comes after months of consideration and work, informed by where schools are financially and what they need. In the background of this back-to-school season, my team and I have been preparing that budget. Everything we see at the surface of our schools – buses transporting students, teachers welcoming kids to their classrooms, and students learning and succeeding – is fueled by the dollars allocated through the K-12 public school budget. Preparing it is a huge responsibility, and in this tight fiscal environment, we had to be agile in finding money and allocating it effectively. We have to look at the pot of money available and find the most efficient ways to use it so districts and charters can maximize their appropriation for the betterment of their students and communities. Here are some things I’d like Idahoans to know about this year’s requested K-12 budget: We prepared this budget knowing that the one-time funding the Legislature appropriated to support high-needs students in FY27 was just that: one-time. Amidst cutbacks and reductions, we successfully funded a new policy with interest from existing accounts. That matters. We were very clear that this wasn’t the long-term fix and that we’d return with another request tied to interest. We had to work again this year to secure funding for FY28. That work meant funding for high-needs students was $1.7 million, rather than zero. Our commitment is unchanged, but the current funding mechanism requires us to return to the negotiation table to receive any support for this much-needed fund. That broken mechanism – the reason we’re negotiating one-time funding instead of ongoing support – is one of the most important issues this budget begins to address. During the 2026 legislative session, my department and I had countless conversations about overhauling Idaho’s public school funding formula, created in 1994. Revising that formula to get the right funding into the right places will help solve problems for high-needs students, our educators, and our educational communities. It will create a flow of money that reflects today’s needs, not 1994’s. To say that work will not come with growing pains would be naïve. That’s why we’re asking for $20 million in new operational funding. Operational funding allows schools to address a variety of needs and, most importantly, is the largest source of dollars used to fund special education services. Your child’s classroom should not have to endure these growing pains. This budget request helps ensure it won’t. This request should also assure taxpayers of one thing: we remain committed to supporting students who need more to succeed while moving toward a solution that eliminates the need for one-time asks and constant negotiation. We want a funding formula that works for Idaho’s modern classrooms, and this budget request is an important step in that direction.

items.body: A voter deposits a mail-in ballot at the drop box outside the Chester County Government Center in Pennsylvania on Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star) Across the country, state election officials are waiting to discover if federal courts will allow the Trump administration’s restrictions on mail-in voting to take effect. In Idaho, like many other states , election officials are nervous the changes might come too close to the 2026 midterm elections, which are less than two months away on Nov. 3. Why the rushed Postal Service plan for mail-in voting has states in a panic The changes — proposed in a new U.S. Postal Service rule that implements an executive order by President Donald Trump — would require federal review of the design of absentee ballots and impose new rules on the design of envelopes containing absentee ballots, among other things. “In the moment, the biggest concern … is just we’re so close to the election,” Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, the state’s top election official and an elected Republican, said in an interview last week. “There’s the practical implications of getting absentee ballots out.” McGrane said he isn’t sure that Idaho or other states would be able to fully comply with the USPS rule if it takes effect before this year’s election. He said county clerks across Idaho, who run the state’s elections, are busy finalizing ballots to print and mail out absentee ballots to military and overseas voters by Sept. 19. In Idaho’s largest county, Ada — which is home to Boise — election officials have told the state they need to know about any changes to ballots by Wednesday in order to make changes before they print the ballots, said Trent Tripple, the Republican elected county clerk for Ada County. He said he also worries about making big changes months before the election. “If you want the most secure election possible, do not put artificial timelines and make us change things at the last second,” he said in an interview. “If you’re doing that, I guarantee you there will be mistakes that are made — because we don’t have the time. We can’t back up an election.” And that’s all on top of other potential ballot changes facing Idaho election officials as the Idaho Supreme Court weighs a lawsuit by the organizers of Proposition 1, an abortion legalization ballot initiative, that challenges state officials’ descriptions of the initiative . (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) The Idaho Supreme Court on Friday unanimously ruled that state officials must redraft explanations of the effect of voting for or against the proposed abortion rights initiative that will appear on voters’ Nov. 3 general election ballots. The court does not have the authority to write new language, but told the offices of the Idaho Attorney General and Secretary of State that they must submit revised ballot language to the court by 5 p.m. Saturday — around 24 hours after the decision was entered. Idaho Supreme Court Justice Gregory Moeller, right, asks a question during a hearing in this April 25, 2025, file photo. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) The decision, written by Justice Gregory Moeller, found that neither the “yes” or “no” effect statements met the law’s requirements. “A statement is not ‘clear’ if it leaves voters uncertain about a principal legal consequence of their choice, and it does not describe ‘the effect’ of a vote if it materially misstates that consequence,” Moeller wrote. “Conciseness permits Respondents to omit unnecessary detail; it does not permit them to convey an inaccurate picture of the effect of a specific vote.” The ballot “effect statements,” required under state law to be a clear and concise explanation of the impacts of a yes or no vote, were written by Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador and Secretary of State Phil McGrane. The state’s high court heard oral arguments Wednesday and issued a speedy ruling as election officials neared a Sept. 11 deadline to be able to send ballots to military and overseas voters. Supporters of the initiative, called Prop 1, filed a lawsuit on Aug. 27, arguing that the drafted effect statements of “yes” or “no” votes on the ballot measure were “misleading” and “confusing.” Attorneys representing Labrador and McGrane defended the statements in court, arguing they were the clearest and shortest way to inform voters. Joe Parris, a spokesperson for the secretary of state, said Friday the office is working to comply with the order. “We appreciate the Idaho Supreme Court’s prompt review of Proposition One yes-and-no effect statements,” Parris said in an email. “As directed by the court, we are working closely with the Attorney General’s Office to prepare and submit revised statements. items.body: Idaho’s abortion ban applies to any stage of pregnancy, with affirmative defenses for cases of rape and incest with an accompanying police report and if an abortion is necessary to save a patient’s life. (Photo illustration by Getty Images) A panel of judges has placed on hold a federal court order protecting an Idaho fetal medicine doctor from prosecution for abortions performed in specific circumstances. The order means Idaho’s abortion laws are fully in effect, with only exemptions to protect the life of the mother, or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester if a police report has been filed. Doctors who perform abortions outside of those exemptions face felony penalties and revocation or suspension of their medical license. Idaho federal judge narrows abortion ruling to only protect Boise doctor who filed lawsuit The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals panel on Thursday blocked a ruling that would’ve carved out new exemptions in Idaho’s strict abortion ban for the doctor challenging the law. The order will be in place until Ninth Circuit judges are scheduled to hear arguments on Sept. 22. Previously, U.S. District of Idaho Court Judge B. Lynn Winmill wrote in an 81-page decision on Aug. 13 that abortions could be performed in cases where the mother faced serious health risks or risk of self-harm, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. However, after Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador appealed the ruling, Winmill n arrowed the decision to only protect the doctor who filed the lawsuit challenging Idaho’s abortion ban, Dr. Stacy Seyb. Seyb, represented by attorneys from the Lawyering Project and Legal Voice, challenged the constitutionality of Idaho abortion ban’s limited exceptions “The Constitution protects pregnant people’s access to life- and health-preserving abortion care,” Lawyering Project Executive Director Stephanie Toti said in an email to the Sun “We are hopeful that the court of appeals will allow that care to resume after it hears oral argument later this month.” Idaho Family Policy Center attorneys file brief in support of law on half of Idaho lawmakers Attorneys with the Idaho Family Policy Center, a conservative Christian lobbying group, filed a brief in support of Idaho’s abortion ban on behalf of 54 Idaho state legislators. Idaho Family Policy Center Legal Director Caleb Pirc wrote that Winmill’s decision went beyond his authority. “The district court improperly made policy for the people of Idaho,” Pirc wrote. “It may have thought its policy was better than the Legislature’s, but that was not its judgment to make.” The brief says that the authority to create abortion policy rests solely with the Legislature. The lawmakers represented by the brief include 37 House representatives and 17 senators, all Republicans, including leaders from both chambers. (Photo courtesy of Todd Wernex/Idaho Department of Lands) State officials announced the temporary closure of seven trails on Thursday due to the Crooked Fire that is burning near Idaho City. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE The fire is burning in steep, rocky and heavily forested terrain about 14 miles northeast of Idaho City, along the North Fork of the Boise River. Idaho Department of Lands officials said the temporary closures are necessary to protect the public and firefighters’ safety as the wildfire continues to burn. The temporary trail closures include: 694, Granite Creek 692, Peg’s Leg 664, Kevin’s Hand 660, North Fork of Thorn 594, Bannock Loop 123, Easter Creek 110, Chuck Wells The closures apply to everyone, including all motorized and nonmotorized recreation users, officials said. “ Please do not enter closed areas or bypass posted closure signs,” Idaho Department of Lands officials wrote in a press release. “Giving firefighters the room they need is critical to yours and their safety and allows them to focus on protecting our communities, property and public lands. ” Need to get in touch? Have a news tip? CONTACT US The seven new temporary trail closures are in addition to existing closures the U.S. Forest Service announced Aug. 23 , which are scheduled to remain in place until Dec. 31 unless rescinded earlier. Those closures affect the Black Rock Campground, Upper Crooked River Trailhead and Lower Crooked River Trailhead, officials said. The Crooked Fire is a human-caused fire that started Aug. 18 outside of Idaho City. The cause of the fire, which has burned 9,956 acres, is under investigation, officials said. Crews are using a full-suppression strategy where conditions allow them to do so safely, officials said. There were about 600 personnel fighting the Crooked Fire as of Thursday, as well as eight helicopters, 22 engines and 14 pieces of heavy equipment, according to Great Basin Incident Management Team 3. Containment was estimated at 21% as of Thursday. items.body: Educators, lawmakers, students and architects gathered in Boise and Star Wednesday to celebrate the groundbreakings of two new schools. The projects will give hundreds of students in the West Ada and Middleton districts new classrooms in 2027 and 2028 — and get some of those students out of portables. The projects have something in common: Neither district passed a local bond measure or increased property taxes to fund them. “The most important thing is that we’re getting this school built,” House Speaker Mike Moyle, R-Star, told EdNews at the Middleton groundbreaking in Star. “The second most important thing is that we’re getting it done without raising property taxes.” Students at a groundbreaking for the rebuilt Lake Hazel Elementary in the West Ada School District on Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026. items.title: Idaho U.S. Senate candidate David Roth removes name from general election ballot
items.summary: This article was first published in the Idaho Capital Sun Idaho Democrat David Roth, who had been running for the U.S. Senate seat held by Idaho Republican Jim Risch, officially withdrew his name from the ballot just days before the deadline. Roth submitted his withdrawal form on Aug. 28, citing a “lack of support from Democratic Party,” according to the form obtained by the Idaho Capital Sun in a
items.body: This article was first published in the Idaho Capital Sun Idaho Democrat David Roth, who had been running for the U.S. Senate seat held by Idaho Republican Jim Risch, officially withdrew his name from the ballot just days before the deadline. Roth submitted his withdrawal form on Aug. 28, citing a “lack of support from Democratic Party,” according to the form obtained by the Idaho Capital Sun in a public records request. A spokesperson for the Idaho Democratic Party declined to comment. Roth faced pressure from fellow Democrats to clear way for independent candidate Roth announced he was ending his campaign on July 28, the Idaho Capital Sun reported. He had faced strong pressure from supporters of independent candidate Todd Achilles, who argued an independent had a better chance of defeating the longtime incumbent in a head-to-head race. Roth did not endorse Achilles. Roth told the Sun he didn’t want to drop out, but he felt like he didn’t have a choice. He’d also received a letter from leaders of Ada County Democrats asking him to drop out , the Spokesman-Review reported. “Without support from Ada County, I mean that really hindered fundraising or campaign ability,” Roth told the Sun in a phone interview. “And when you have so many people who hold leadership positions in the party advocating for a candidate besides their nominee, it makes it really just impossible.” Roth’s most recent federal election filing shows he garnered about $14,600 in contributions but that his campaign had about $10,100 in debts and loans to be paid back, as of June 30. Roth ran for federal office in 2022 and 2024 and for the state Legislature in 2020. He said this run was “probably the worst experience I’ve ever been through in my entire life.” “And I’ve been through a lot,” he said. He expressed disappointment in his party leaders for not supporting the Democratic nominee in the race after he won his primary contest in May. “It’s an unfortunate situation,” he said. “I think the Democratic voters of Idaho have really lost their opportunity to have a voice, and I think it just goes to show how broken our whole system is.” Achilles’ most recent campaign finance filing shows he’s raised nearly $700,000, although his campaign has recently advertised he’s collected over $1 million. Risch’s warchest was more than $4.4 million as of June 30. The Federal Election Commission requires quarterly reporting on campaign contributions and expenditures, and the next filing deadline is Oct. 15. Without Roth’s formal withdrawal, his name would’ve still appeared on the Nov. 3 general election ballot. Achilles’ campaign has repeatedly said his odds are better if the contest is between him and Risch. “I respect Roth running and making the decision that the campaign just didn’t have the resources it needed to be competitive,” Achilles said in an interview. “I think it’s all about being competitive.” After Roth’s withdrawal, Achilles said his campaign’s plan is to, “keep doing what we’re doing, which is just being out there talking Idahoans and you know working hard on a campaign.” Risch in an interview for an August story told the Sun he was not concerned after Roth announced his departure from the race. “I know people are getting excited all of a sudden because I was running against two Democrats, and now I’m running against one Democrat,” Risch said, referencing that Achilles previously was a Democratic state legislator. “I’ve done that all my life.” Risch, Achilles, independent Natalie Fleming and Libertarian Matt Loesby will appear on ballots for the U.S. Senate race. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) As the deadline to print ballots looms, the Idaho Supreme Court will decide whether state officials’ descriptions of the effects of voting for or against a proposed abortion rights initiative will appear on ballots in November. The justices questioned the state officials’ attorneys and the legal challengers Wednesday about how best to ensure voters are informed about the ballot measure that would repeal Idaho’s abortion bans if passed. Idaho Secretary of State candidate Phil McGrane talks with a supporter during the Idaho Republican Party primary celebration on May 17, 2022. (Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) Attorneys for supporters of the initiative argued before the court Wednesday that the “yes” and “no” effect statements drafted by Republicans Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador and Secretary of State Phil McGrane were misleading and confusing. Attorneys for Labrador and McGrane said the two elected officials did their due diligence to comply with the state law requiring “clear and concise” ballot statements to tell voters what effect their votes would have. The proposed, voter-led ballot initiative would legalize abortion until fetal viability or in cases of emergency, and enumerate reproductive rights, including access to contraception and IVF, and rights to privacy in medical decision-making. What does the draft ballot language say? The effect statements, as drafted by state officials, are: “A YES vote would create reproductive rights, including a right to abortion before a fetus’s ability to survive and after a fetus’s ability to survive in cases of a medical emergency, and provide liability protections for healthcare providers.” “A NO vote would make no change to Idaho’s current law, which protects the life of the unborn while allowing abortion in reported cases of rape or incest, or when necessary to protect the life of the mother.” Melanie Folwell, lead organizer for the ballot initiative in Idaho to restore abortion access, speaks to supporters at the Idaho Capitol in July. (Photo by Kelcie Moseley-Morris/Stateline) Idahoans United for Women and Families, the nonprofit organization that drafted the initiative — now called Proposition 1 — filed the lawsuit challenging the ballot language on Aug. 27, Stateline reported. The lawsuit argues the proposed language is confusing, especially the description of the existing abortion ban, which the attorneys say is incomplete. The deadline for the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office to mail printed ballots and voter information pamphlets is Sept. 18 and Sept. 25, respectively, according to court filings. “The top priority is making sure that there is clear language on the ballot, that is what we have fought for since the beginning,” Melanie Folwell, lead organizer for the initiative proponents Idahoans United, told the Idaho Capital Sun following the hearing. items.body: Idaho's state prison system formally entered into an agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. It's the second state agency to enter the 287(g) program. (Photo by Mia Maldonado/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s state prison system has entered into a formal agreement with federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE. It’s the second state agency to join the federal immigration program. The Idaho Department of Correction on Aug. 28 joined the 287(g ) program, which allows local law enforcement to carry out some limited immigration enforcement with supervision from federal authorities, according to ICE records of participating agencies. Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little gives his State of the State Address from the House chambers on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “Idaho has a responsibility to uphold the rule of law and protect the people of our state,” Gov. Brad Little said in a press release. “This agreement gives Idaho another tool to make sure criminal aliens who are subject to federal immigration enforcement are transferred to federal custody when they have completed their Idaho sentences. Idaho will continue working with the Trump administration to secure our communities and support the enforcement of our nation’s laws.” The state prison agency’s agreement follows what’s called the “warrant service” model, which allows designated officers within the agency to serve warrants to undocumented people in custody. The agreement “formalizes a process IDOC has already been using to assist ICE,” according to a press release from the governor’s office. Correction staff have historically provided ICE with information on inmates with felony convictions to allow the federal agents to identify those who may be subject to immigration detainers, which are requests by ICE to hold individuals to prevent the release of people who may be undocumented, the release said. Bree Derrick (Photo from Idaho Department of Correction) “IDOC has a longstanding responsibility to coordinate with our federal partners when individuals in our custody are subject to federal immigration enforcement,” IDOC Director Bree Derrick said in the press release. “This agreement strengthens that coordination and gives our department a clear, formal process for serving ICE warrants and transferring individuals into federal custody when their Idaho sentences are complete.” The state prison agency also “facilitates due process hearings for individuals undergoing deportation proceedings and coordinates with ICE when Idaho sentences are satisfied,” the release said. In June 2025 , Idaho State Police entered a 287(g) agreement with ICE to help transport state inmates to federal detention facilities for deportation. This agreement was funded by the governor’s office emergency funds. As of May, ISP had transported more than 80 people out of correctional facilities, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. An Idaho Capital Sun analysis found some cases where charges were dismissed or still pending when the person was transported to an ICE facility. ISP leaders later said the agency changed its procedure to ensure convictions were secured before transporting individuals. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. items.body: The Kootenai County prosecutor’s office said last week there’s no update on a complaint that the Lakeland School Board again voted on an unnoticed agenda item. EdNews filed the complaint last month after trustees voted on “Item E” following a July 29 executive session, a closed portion of a public meeting. The item was not listed as an action item, and no details were posted. Idaho Code 74-204(4) requires an agenda to identify an item as an “action item” when it requires a vote, providing notice to the public that action may be taken. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) Months after protestors wouldn’t leave the lobby of the Idaho governor’s office in an attempt to meet with him over anti-transgender bills, a jury on Tuesday found a local minister guilty on a misdemeanor trespassing charge. The jury found the Rev. Sara LaWall — who wore a clerical collar under a rainbow speckled blazer as she sat in court — guilty of trespassing after prosecutors said she remained in the governor’s office after being warned it was closed for the night during a protest of anti-trans bills this spring. Idaho’s transgender bathroom ban is now the law. How will police enforce it? That’s still unclear. After the jury delivered the verdict, LaWall, the minister for the Boise Unitarian Universalist Fellowship, told reporters that the possible prison sentence she could face would be less time than judges can dole out for violations of Idaho’s new criminal transgender bathroom ban . “That just feels wholly unfair and outsized and ridiculous,” LaWall told reporters after her trial. “… The jury found me guilty of staying in the governor’s office after being told to leave. I didn’t dispute those facts. But someone going to the bathroom now has a higher sentence, and that just feels so disproportionate and so wrong.” Under state law , her trespassing charge is punishable by up to six months in prison. The state’s bathroom ban allows for up to a year in prison on a first offense and up to five years on repeat offenses. Minutes after the nearly full-day trial finished Tuesday, the jury reached its verdict. LaWall will be sentenced on the charge later. Idaho 4th District Judge Adam Kimball scheduled her sentencing for Sept. 17. LaWall’s attorney requested her sentencing be delayed instead of issued Tuesday evening. She hopes at her sentencing she can share more about why she was at the governor’s office. “I have really mixed feelings,” LaWall said of the verdict. “It’s hard not to feel a little emotional about the verdict, but I don’t — I’m not entirely surprised. I took the stand and said as much as the judge allowed me to say about why we were there, which wasn’t very much, and that was disappointing to me to not be able to tell more of the story about why we were there.” LaWall was one of nine protestors who were arrested on trespassing charges at the April 1 protest. At the protest, LaWall and others waited in the lobby in the governor’s office for more than three hours. The protest came a day after Gov. Brad Little signed into law what advocates call the most extreme criminal transgender bathroom ban in the nation. Protestors were also attempting to meet with him and urge him to veto a bill that requires teachers and doctors to out transgender minors to their parents , or face lawsuits. items.body: Every two years, something unusual happens in Idaho: every single member of the Legislature is up for election. All 70 members of the Idaho House face the voters. So do all 35 members of the Idaho Senate. That means every legislator in Boise operates on essentially the same political clock. Every two years, every seat is on the ballot, every incumbent is potentially campaigning, and every member knows the next primary is never far away. We should change that. Idaho should keep two-year terms for members of the House but move state senators to four-year terms, staggered so roughly half the Senate is elected every two years. It would make the Senate more deliberative, provide greater continuity in state government, reduce some of the election-year incentives for political theater and strengthen the Legislature’s ability to serve as a check on the permanent bureaucracy. Most importantly, it would create a meaningful institutional difference between Idaho’s two legislative chambers. After all, if we’re going to have a House and a Senate, they shouldn’t simply be two versions of the same thing. The Idaho Constitution currently gives representatives and senators the same two-year terms. The House is larger and the Senate smaller, but members of both chambers face voters on precisely the same schedule. That’s not how most states do it. And there is a reason. The two chambers of a legislature are supposed to serve somewhat different purposes. The House should be the chamber closest to the people and most immediately responsive to shifts in public opinion. Its members should return to voters frequently. Two-year terms make sense. The Senate should be different. A Senate is traditionally the smaller and more deliberative legislative body. Its members should have greater opportunity to take a longer view, develop expertise and provide continuity as political winds change. That doesn’t make senators more important than representatives. It gives them a different institutional role. Consider the political life of a newly elected Idaho senator. Win an election in November. Go to Boise in January. Serve one legislative session. Spend the interim knowing another election is approaching. Return for a second session—and by then the primary election is only months away. Then start all over again. There is barely time to govern before it’s time to campaign. Today, every one of Idaho’s 105 legislative seats appears on the ballot at the same time. Theoretically, a single election could send 105 brand-new legislators to Boise. Some Idahoans might hear that and say: Good. There is something appealing about a clean sweep. Turnover can bring fresh ideas, disrupt comfortable relationships and remind elected officials that the offices they occupy belong to the people. But there is another side to that equation. If every legislator is new, state government isn’t. The agencies are still there. The departments are still there. The administrative rules, budget processes and government programs are still there. And the career employees who have spent years—or decades—working inside that system are still there. One of the Legislature’s most important responsibilities is overseeing the executive branch and the permanent bureaucracy beneath it. Lawmakers control appropriations, write the laws agencies implement and are supposed to ask hard questions on behalf of taxpayers. To do that effectively, legislators need expertise of their own. That’s an important point for those of us who believe in limited government. Limiting government isn’t only about asking how much power government possesses. We should also care about where that power resides and who exercises it. (Photo by Valentin Termite/Idaho Capital Sun) Congressman Russ Fulcher, R-Idaho (Photo courtesy of Russ Fulcher’s official website) Idaho Republican U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher signed on to federal legislation to limit federal law enforcement’s access to data from automated license plate readers, like Flock cameras, and other surveillance equipment. Fulcher announced Monday in a press release that he is co-sponsoring H.R. 9716 , called the Protecting Rights in Video and Equipment Acquired Discovery Act, or Privacy Act. The legislation would, in most cases, require federal law enforcement to obtain a warrant from a federal judge before accessing surveillance data from state and local systems, including cameras that capture images of vehicle occupants, long-range microphones, electronic fingerprint detection technology, and “substantially similar technology” as determined by the U.S. attorney general, according to the press release. “I’m proud to sign on to this legislation to protect the privacy rights of Idahoans from increasingly intrusive surveillance data collection and to prohibit the widespread deployment of such surveillance tools with federal dollars,” Fulcher said in the press release. “It’s simple: if the federal government wants to access state and local systems’ data on citizens, they need to get a warrant.” The legislation would also put time limits on the retention of data federal authorities obtained, unless a court authorizes an extension or the data is needed as evidence for ongoing prosecution. The bill would also prohibit federal funds from being used to purchase or install surveillance devices, with some exceptions for systems used solely for toll collections on federally funded highways, school violence prevention programs, grants provided under the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act, and portable systems for specific law enforcement operations with a warrant. The bill, brought by Texas Republican U.S. Rep. Keith Self, was introduced July 15 and has not yet been voted on by a committee. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Idahoans have expressed concerns about surveillance cameras A number of Idaho cities statewide have contracts for automated license plate readers, called ALPRs, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. Flock is the most common and well-known brand of this type of camera. In July, nearly 100 residents filled the Caldwell City Council chambers, and about a dozen of them spoke about their concern about the city’s use of Flock cameras , the Idaho Press reported. All eyes on Flock as Idaho navigates surveillance technology across the state A 2025 Idaho state law prevents these readers from being used for anything other than “the investigation of felony, misdemeanor crimes, traffic accidents or to search for missing or endangered persons.” However, Twin Falls cameras were searched at least 631 times in March, May and June of 2026 for immigration-related searches, the Sun reported. The searches originated from outside Idaho, and later the Twin Falls Police Department changed its network sharing policies to avoid inadvertently running afoul of Idaho law and its own restrictions on immigration searches. In March, then-Jerome County Sheriff George Oppedyk used Flock cameras to search for his wife’s vehicle hundreds of times between July and September 2025, KMVT reported. Oppedyk retired in April. In early August, the Washington Post reported that at least 50 law enforcement officers across the nation had been charged with or accused of misusing the cameras to track women. Fulcher’s office regularly polls constituents who email him, and recent polls found that data privacy was one of their top concerns, Fulcher told the Idaho Capital Sun in an Aug. 12 interview. “The data privacy stuff, especially recently with the Flock cameras, that has got a lot of people on edge,” Fulcher said. But before it was mounted at the state’s Capitol, the bell toured the state on the back of a pickup truck. And as Americans commemorate the nation’s 250th birthday this year, Idaho’s Liberty Bell is headed back on tour . “We want to have people experience the birth of a nation,” Idaho Treasurer Julie Ellsworth said in an interview. “… We want a memorable thing that touches every place of Idaho.” The tour starts Wednesday with a round of stops in East Idaho, starting in Pocatello and working its way further east, before visiting each of the state’s 44 counties. But how did Idaho even get its own version of the Liberty Bell? The bell — modeled after the cracked original in Philadelphia that has become a national symbol — was one of many cast and given to states in an effort to sell U.S. savings bonds, according to a history of the bell prepared by the Idaho State Historical Society. State officials designed this tour to mimic the original tour of the bell from 76 years ago. On its journey across Idaho, the state’s Liberty Bell will sit on the rear axle of a flatbed Ford F-450 pickup. The state is leasing the custom truck for free from Kendall Ford, an auto dealer in the Boise area, Ellsworth said. The new truck has a few more bells and whistles than the original truck had — like enhanced suspension and Spudjamin Franklin, one of many “Revolutionary Spuds” that the state treasurer created to celebrate America’s 250th anniversary. But it’s also missing something that the original truck, a custom Ford R-5 flatbed, had: a loudspeaker, which was used to promote the sale of U.S. savings bonds, according to Janet Gallimore, the executive director of the Idaho State Historical Society, which cares for the state’s artifacts and helped plan the bell’s recent restoration. The 1950 tour of Idaho’s replica of the Liberty Bell was to promote the sale of U.S. savings bonds. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho State Treasurer’s Office) “I … just love the symbology of the bell and what it means, what it meant for obviously the beginnings of our country and the founding of our country, but what that idea of liberty, justice, self-government means to people today. Because it’s a powerful symbol of those things that make us American,” she said in an interview. On the road, the bell will be encased in a cloth cover. At its stops in each county, it will remain on the bed of the truck for display. When will Idaho’s Liberty Bell be near you? Officials aren’t releasing a daily schedule of where the bell will be in each town at a given time until closer to the dates. (Photo by Jacob Fischler/States Newsroom) A Massachusetts federal judge on Monday declined the Trump administration’s request to overturn the temporary restraining order she signed last week that blocks the U.S. Postal Service from carrying out a r
items.body: A ballot drop box in Kitsap County, Washington, pictured Aug. 29, 2026. Washington is one of the eight states that conducts elections entirely by mail. (Photo by Jacob Fischler/States Newsroom) A Massachusetts federal judge on Monday declined the Trump administration’s request to overturn the temporary restraining order she signed last week that blocks the U.S. Postal Service from carrying out a rule placing new restrictions on mail-in voting. The 14-day order published Aug. 27 was not appealable, U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani wrote in a brief order Monday . But even if the order could be appealed, the administration would lose on the merits, Talwani wrote. “It is likely that the USPS lacked authority to issue the Final Rule and that the Final Rule is substantively unconstitutional and contrary to law,” she wrote. She dismissed the administration’s argument that the temporary restraining order came too close to Election Day as a “cynical interpretation” of the U.S. Supreme Court’s Aug. 24 decision that allowed President Donald Trump’s related executive order to move forward on procedural grounds. The high court found that Trump’s executive order, which directed the Postal Service to create the rule, could not be challenged until the rule itself was in place. It made no determination on the merits of the rule. “A Final Rule has now issued and, contrary to Defendants’ cynical interpretation, the Supreme Court has not endorsed the view that any challenge to the Final Rule is now too late,” Talwani, whom President Barack Obama appointed to the bench, wrote. She added that she disagreed with the USPS argument that the requirements of the rule, which would force states to overhaul their vote-by-mail systems ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections and to gain federal government approval of lists of voters who requested mail ballots, were “modest.” The administration is also fighting Democratic-led states and voting rights groups in the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals over Talwani’s temporary restraining order and in Talwani’s court over a longer pause of the final rule. Several Republican state attorneys general, representing Alabama, Florida, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota and Texas, joined the suit on the federal government’s side. The rule’s challengers say it is an inappropriate incursion of states’ power to administer elections, and would likely disenfranchise people who depend on mail ballots to vote. Trump has long claimed, without evidence, and despite his personal use of the service, that mail voting enables election fraud. The administration has said its rule is needed to ensure that noncitizens do not vote in federal elections, which studies have shown is rare. Trump issued the executive order March 31. States and voting rights groups immediately sued to stop it, but the legal battle heated up last week with the Supreme Court’s procedural decision on its emergency docket. The states and groups challenging the law quickly refiled their lawsuits to reflect that the rule had been published Aug. 21.

items.body: Boise State University is denying wrongdoing in a public records dispute with a conservative lobbying group. Attorneys for Boise State say the university “acted in good faith” in responding to the Idaho Family Policy Center — even though the group received only two pages of university records, at a cost of $257.02. The IFPC filed a lawsuit on July 24 , stemming from a seven-month records dispute. The Christian lobbying group requested documents, data and correspondence related to a 2025 article authored by two Boise State researchers. The article said 35% of OB-GYNs left Idaho between 2022 and 2024, in the wake of the state’s near-total ban on abortion. The IFPC authored one of Idaho’s anti-abortion laws. The lawsuit alleges Boise State dragged out its response to the request for more than a month, withheld germane documents and charged for a costly legal review of the records that ultimately were released. “By refusing multiple requests for these documents, and rebuffing efforts to solve this matter without litigation, BSU has frivolously pursued its refusal,” the IFPC said in its lawsuit. In a response filed Tuesday, Boise State said it produced all documents that fell within the parameters of the request and did not delay its response. The university also defended the bill that it sent to the IFPC — which reflected 6.5 hours of staff review, including 3 hours of legal work. Idaho’s public records law is based in a presumption of openness. In other words, documents are considered public records unless they are specifically exempt from disclosure. The dispute between Boise State and the IFPC centers on two intertwined issues. The timing . The law requires public entities to release records to Idaho residents within three working days — although agencies can and frequently do claim an extension that pushes the timetable to 10 working days. In this case, IFPC policy analyst Grace Howat filed a records request on Dec. 10. Boise State responded on Dec. 23, within 10 working days. The university did not produce the records at this time, but instead sent an estimate — reflecting the potential cost of reviewing and producing the records. Boise State did not request payment at this time. On Jan. 8, Boise State sent a $257.02 invoice. IFPC paid the bill that day. Howat twice sent followup emails, asking about the status of the records request. “Am I able to receive the records I requested and paid for?” she wrote on Jan. 26. The university provided the two-page response on Jan. 27 — more than 10 working days after IFPC paid the invoice. But in Boise State’s response in court, attorneys defended the turnaround time. “(Boise State) denies (IFPC’s) characterization that (Boise State) ‘sat on the request for over a month.’” Carsten Peterson and Eric Stokes are representing Boise State in the case. They work for Hawley Troxell , a Boise-based firm prominent in education law . The invoice . Public agencies are required to cover some cost of retrieving records — their first two hours of staff time and the first 100 pages of paper records. Beyond that, agencies are allowed to bill their costs, but they aren’t required to do so. Boise State says the $257.02 invoice covers 6.5 hours of staff review, above the two “free” hours of employee time. IFPC is skeptical, noting that the two pages released by Boise State were unredacted. In their response, Boise State’s attorneys say that staff had to review documents beyond the two pages that were released. “(Boise State) denies the inference that 6 1/2 hours responding to Ms. Howat’s request was excessive.” What’s next? items.body: Crews are completing the new Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass south of Montpelier in Bear Lake County. (Photo by Julia Barton/Greater Yellowstone Coalition) Correction: This story was corrected to reflect that highway wildlife underpasses have also been built north of Bonners Ferry. Crews are nearing completion of a new wildlife underpass in southeast Idaho after the public, nonprofit agencies, conservation groups and government agencies pushed for years to protect migrating wildlife herds and drivers. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE The Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass is expected to be completed this fall along U.S. Highway 30, south of Montpelier in Bear Lake County, public officials and conservationists announced jointly this week. The wildlife crossing features three underpasses, as well as extensive fencing on either side of the project to direct animals like deer to the wildlife crossing. “We were seeing just all kinds of problems there; we were losing at least 100 deer a year,” Idaho Transportation Department public information officer Justin Smith said in an interview Wednesday. “Over 10 years, that is 1,000 animals we know we lost.” Officials also said those collisions cost drivers and taxpayers millions of dollars every year. “Our primary concern is the safety of the traveling public. Whether they are going through a construction zone or whether they are in a wildlife area, we want to keep people safe on our highways, and this is part of that effort,” Smith said. The Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass represents a partnership between the Idaho Transportation Department, Idaho Department of Fish and Game, the Greater Yellowstone Coalition, the Idaho Conservation League and Bear Lake County, officials said. This map depicts the project area for the Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass near Montpelier. (Map courtesy of Greater Yellowstone Coalition) “Rocky Point shows what’s possible when agencies, conservation and sporting groups and local communities work toward the same goal,” Matt Lucia, Idaho conservation manager at the Greater Yellowstone Coalition, said in a written statement. “(The Greater Yellowstone Coalition) has been part of this project for years — contributing time, energy and funds toward the effort. The next step is making sure the federal funding that made this project possible stays available.” To build the crossing, the Idaho Transportation Department secured a $20.8 million grant from the Federal Highway Administration’s Wildlife Crossing Pilot Program. Funding comes from the federal Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act that was passed by Congress and signed into law by former President Joe Biden in 2021. The federal grant was estimated to cover 98% of the construction costs, but the project may come in under budget, allowing the state to return some of the money to the Federal Highway Administration, Smith said. Idaho’s first major highway wildlife crossing was built outside of Boise in 2023 Need to get in touch? Have a news tip? CONTACT US The Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass near Montpelier is one of a handful of wildlife highway crossing in Idaho. In 2023, crews built the Cervidae Peak Wildlife Overpass on Idaho Highway 21 near Lucky Peak, between Boise and Idaho City. The Cervidae overpass features more than one mile of big game fencing to direct the animals to the safe crossing. Fish and Game officials installed a wildlife camera at the crossing to document how it is working. In 2024, state officials posted a time-lapse video showing more than 1,000 deer safely using the Cervidae Peak Wildlife Overpass between Oct. 17, 2024, and Dec. 18, 2024. In the early 2000s, crews also built wildlife underpasses north of Bonners Ferry on U.S. Highway 95 when they widened the highway, the Spokesman-Review reported. Smith said officials with the Idaho Transportation Department are studying other highway corridors with heavy wildlife populations, and the state is open to pursuing other new wildlife crossings as well.

(Getty Images) An advisory group has identified Idaho counties at high risk for opioid use disorder to target in its recommendations for the state’s use of opioid settlement funds. The Idaho Behavioral Health Council brings together the state’s three branches of government — legislative, judicial and executive — to provide recommendations to lawmakers about how to improve mental health and substance use issues statewide. The council on Friday finalized its recommendation that opioid settlement funds be prioritized for at-risk populations and communities. A summary highlighting some of the counties facing the highest risk of opioid use disorder included Kootenai, Benewah, Nez Perce, Bannock, Bear Lake, Clearwater, Boise and Ada counties. The state’s opioid settlement fund was created from a nationwide settlement with opioid manufacturers and may be used for certain, approved prevention or treatment projects. Last year, the Legislature approved spending $6.8 million of opioid settlement funds, according to a memo from the Division of Financial Management. Idaho Behavioral Health Council asks lawmakers to prioritize rural communities with opioid funding The council voted on its top priorities at a meeting in June, which included funding proposed for projects that focus on prevention for high-risk populations, behavioral health support for first responders, and developing the behavioral health workforce. Council members on Friday agreed to send a one-page summary outlining risk factors for opioid use disorder and highlighting which counties were most at-risk, using a 2024 report titled the Opioid-Related Overdose Vulnerability in Idaho: An Epidemiological Assessment. “This handout identifies risk factors for opioid use disorder and puts them in the context of Idaho, where those places are, where we may have more vulnerable folks, where we have had higher levels of overdose, where we have high levels of opioid prescriptions being written,” said Sara Omundson, administrative director of state courts and co-chair of the Behavioral Health Council. “All of this is based on research that was done over the last few years.” The council also agreed to ask the governor and state legislative budget writers to prioritize projects that serve rural communities in the state. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE What areas are at high risk for opioid use? Factors that may lead to certain populations to be at higher risk of misusing opioids include lower educational attainment, according to the risk factor summary the council included with its recommendations. Those without college experience are almost twice as likely to misuse opioids, the summary said. The summary also identified other Idaho counties at-risk because of factors such as high prescription rates and high narcotic arrests using data from the American Community Survey , the Idaho Prescription Drug Monitoring Program , and the Idaho State Police Statistical Analysis Center. The top counties at risk based on low average educational attainment are Shoshone, Lincoln, Minidoka, Owyhee, Adams, Benewah, Payette, Gooding, Jerome and Clark counties. The top counties for high opioid prescription rates are Nez Perce, Bannock, Bear Lake, Butte, Lewis, Shoshone, Benewah, Caribou, Gem and Lemhi. (Photo by Christophe Paul/U.S. Department of Agriculture) Three Democratic U.S. senators are demanding the Trump Administration investigate reports that Undersecretary of Agriculture for Natural Resources and Environment Michael Boren allegedly pushed officials for additional resources to fight a small wildfire near his Idaho ranch this summer. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE U.S. Sens. Ron Wyden, D-Oregon; Amy Klobuchar, D-Minnesota; and Martin Heinrich, D-New Mexico, requested a full investigation into Boren’s involvement and influence in the Cabin Creek Fire in a letter they sent to U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins. “Mr. Boren’s actions constitute potentially a misuse of taxpayer funds and put American families at further risk by diverting scarce resources from high-priority wildfires threatening communities elsewhere in the region and country,” the senators wrote. “We request a full investigation into the nature and extent of Boren’s involvement in response to the Cabin Creek Fire and a detailed accounting of the safeguards the agency has implemented or plans to implement to prevent political interference and conflicts of interest in wildfire response.” Need to get in touch? Have a news tip? CONTACT US Earlier this month, the Washington Post reported that Boren pushed U.S. Forest Service officials to increase the number of aircraft responding to a small fire near a ranch Boren owns in the Sawtooth National Recreation Area. “Western states are already facing a shortage of firefighting personnel and resources as a direct result of the Trump administration’s staffing and funding cuts,” the Democrats wrote in a press release issued Friday. “During this record setting fire season, fires of much larger size threatening American lives and homes have not received even a fraction of the same commitment of resources.” Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit legal watchdog group, has also called for an investigation into the allegations and filed a complaint with the Agriculture Department’s Office of Inspector General, according to an Aug. 17 press release. “The Inspector General must investigate whether Undersecretary Boren risked public safety to protect his property,” said CREW President Donald K. Sherman in the release. “Not only are Boren’s priorities in doubt, but his actions raise questions about his ‘scant’ qualifications for his role. His reported actions could be the result of incompetence, deliberate malfeasance or both. Regardless, they are inexcusable.” Boren is a founder of Clearwater Analytics, a Boise-based financial technology company. In 2025 President Donald Trump appointed Boren as undersecretary of natural resources and the environment at the U.S. Department of Agriculture. From left to right: Mary Jane Miles, Cheryl Horn, Abigail Echo-Hawk and Eugenia Charles-Newton. (Screenshot via YouTube/House Appropriations Committee) Idaho Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson this year is looking to boost federal funding for tribes to address the ongoing Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons crisis. Chairman of the Interior, Environment and Related Agencies subcommittee U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson, R-Idaho, looks on during a House Appropriations Committee hearing at the Rayburn House Office Building on April 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Heather Diehl/Getty Images) Simpson chairs the Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies Subcommittee of the House Appropriations Committee. The subcommittee in June advanced a budget with a 26% increase to the Bureau of Indian Affairs, which includes: an additional $142 million for criminal investigations and police services $17 million for law enforcement special initiatives $33 million specifically for missing and murdered Indigenous women, which is about a $14.5 million increase over the fiscal year 2026 appropriation. $5 million for the use of forensic genealogy to identify missing and murdered individuals in unsolved cases through the bureau’s Operation Spirit Return. “We put a bunch more money into tribal justice, and that’s hard in a year when we’re trying to reduce spending at the federal level,” Simpson said in an interview. As a result, he said other portions of the budget, such as funding for the Bureau of Land Management, the U.S. Forest Service and the Smithsonian Institution all saw reductions. “But I’ve said from the beginning: We’re not going to try to balance the budget on the back of the tribes,” Simpson said. “These are trust and treaty responsibilities we’ve got with our Native American brothers and sisters, and we’ve got to keep those. ” Coeur d’Alene Tribe Chairman Chief J. Allan told the Idaho Capital Sun in an emailed statement that the tribe supports the effort. “The issue has gotten more attention in recent years, and Congressman Simpson recognizes that serious problems require adequate funding,” Allan said. “While the focus on MMIP is critical, he also recognizes that the tragic situation is the direct result of decades of public safety and justice deficiencies across Indian Country. Addressing those shortfalls across the system will help improve conditions overall, as well as prevent missing and murdered incidents in the future.” Marco Ovando, spokesman for the Shoshone-Paiute Tribes, said there was still a lot of work to be done to address the MMIP crisis. “The crisis of Missing and Murdered Indigenous People within Idaho and the United States is still largely being unaddressed despite national attention in recent years,” Ovando wrote in an emailed statement from the Tribes. “While the Idaho Legislature has created a taskforce in 2020 and a report 2021, state-tribal collaboration remains very limited. … We have a case as recent as this spring where the investigation has produced very little resulting in families without closure, frustrated leadership, and a community left on edge. We hope Congress will appropriate more funding to address these shortfalls because our people are tired of the pain and sorrow and lack of help.” Leaders from the Nez Perce, Shoshone-Bannock, and Kootenai Tribes could not be reached for comment. items.body: Melanie Folwell, lead organizer for the ballot initiative in Idaho to restore abortion access, speaks to supporters at the Idaho Capitol in July. The nonprofit she leads, Idahoans United for Women and Families, is suing the state over a final segment of ballot language that will also appear in the statewide voter pamphlet. (Photo by Kelcie Moseley-Morris/Stateline) BOISE, Idaho — The group leading the effort to restore abortion access by ballot initiative in Idaho has filed a lawsuit against state officials over proposed language that will appear on the ballot and in a state-issued voter pamphlet. Idahoans United for Women and Families, the nonprofit organization that drafted the initiative — now called Proposition 1 — says the “yes” and “no” statements as prepared by Idaho officials violate the law guiding the initiative process and are confusing and misleading. Attorneys filed the lawsuit to the Idaho Supreme Court late Wednesday night. Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane stressed that the issue needs to be quickly resolved to meet upcoming ballot deadlines. The voter pamphlet must be printed by September 25, according to the law, and ballots need to be mailed to military and overseas voters about a week before that. McGrane said the state has paused production amid the litigation on the 850,000 copies of the voter pamphlet that need to be printed and mailed. “There was a good-faith effort to try and reflect each of the sides of the pro and con statements that were submitted to us,” McGrane told Stateline by phone on Thursday. “I think one of the biggest challenges that we’re going to see with Proposition 1 is that it’s a very complicated issue with a lot of nuance … and this isn’t a simple issue to consolidate down into a short, one-sentence statement.” Following the law, McGrane developed the language for the statements with Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador, who has been outspoken in his anti-abortion views for many years and recently appealed a federal judge’s decision that would protect abortion access in cases of threats to a pregnant patient’s physical and mental health. Labrador told Stateline in an emailed statement that his duty alongside the secretary was to clearly and concisely explain the effects of a “yes” or “no” vote and to fully inform Idaho voters, and said they applied the same legal standard to every measure that has been on the ballot. “Idaho voters deserve a straightforward explanation of what their vote will do,” Labrador said. Idaho Supreme Court orders officials to revise abortion ballot initiative language, impact statement There have been similar legal fights over abortion ballot language in other states. Activists on both sides of the issue in Missouri, for example, have spent years arguing over ballot language , both on the 2024 citizen-led amendment that restored legal access to abortion, and on the 2026 amendment referred by the legislature that would reinstate the ban. Similar battles between Republican state officials and initiative organizers played out in Ohio , Arizona and Montana between 2023 and 2024. Voters in all three of those states ultimately approved amendments to protect abortion rights. It’s also not the first time Idahoans United for Women and Families has sued the state over ballot language. In April 2025, the Idaho Supreme Court heard arguments in the lawsuit, including whether the short ballot title and fiscal impact statement should be revised, and unanimously sided with Idahoans United on those two elements.
