items.body: Cynthia Pemberton was working the Statehouse — meeting with lawmakers, trying to line up votes — when she passed House Speaker Mike Moyle in a hallway. Lewis-Clark State College President Cynthia Pemberton. (Kevin Richert/Idaho EdNews) " data-large-file="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Pemberton-1.27.25-1180x885.jpg" class="wp-image-100675 size-large" src="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Pemberton-1.27.25-1180x885.jpg" alt="" width="1180" height="885" srcset="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Pemberton-1.27.25-1180x885.jpg 1180w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Pemberton-1.27.25-620x465.jpg 620w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Pemberton-1.27.25-200x150.jpg 200w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Pemberton-1.27.25-1536x1152.jpg 1536w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Pemberton-1.27.25.jpg 1920w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1180px) 100vw, 1180px" /> Lewis-Clark State College President Cynthia Pemberton addresses the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee in January 2025. (Kevin Richert/Idaho EdNews) Heading to a meeting, flanked by House GOP Caucus Chair Jaron Crane, Moyle wasted no time getting to the point — Pemberton’s bill to rebrand Lewis-Clark State College as the state’s fourth full-fledged university. “He commented in passing that he hadn’t had time to ‘kill it yet,’” Pemberton, LC State’s president, said in subsequent emails to two other lawmakers. Pemberton stands by her account. When EdNews asked Moyle about the exchange this week, he chuckled. “She was persistent in the hallway all the time. I was just giving her a hard time.” Either way, the bill died, without a House hearing. Moyle, R-Star, insists he didn’t kill it, but says he doesn’t support the name change. Pemberton pledges to try again in 2027. “I better try one more time,” Pemberton said in an EdNews interview last week. “The campus community wants me to try again.” While renaming sounds cosmetic and simple, branding is essential. Supporters say university status better reflects a 133-year-old institution offering everything from associate’s degrees to master’s programs. A name is how an institution of higher learning markets itself to would-be students, prospective faculty members and possible business partners. A one-word change can change a lot. And the LC State renaming proposal was the most significant higher ed policy bill from the 2026 session. Emails between Pemberton and legislators — obtained by Idaho Education News through a public records request — offer an unusual and unfiltered behind-the-scenes look at how this bill died. The name change sailed through the Senate, but ran into high-placed resistance in the House, from Moyle and from his newly appointed House Education Committee chairman. LC State officials lobbied furiously to save their bill — working their skeptics, directly and indirectly — but to no avail. The case for the change With a freshly made video and handouts, and a webpage dedicated to the name change initiative , LC State is giving an updated look to the rebranding proposal. Fundamentally, the bullet points haven’t changed. A rebrand aligns LC State with Idaho’s four-year universities — and distinguishes LC State from the public two-year schools that have “college” in their name. University status brings LC State in line with other teaching-oriented institutions in the West. It would help LC State compete with a new wave of competition: out-of-state online schools with “university” in their title. Pemberton sees it as simple marketing. A car dealership wouldn’t want its sign to list only one make of car when it has multiple options on the lot. The same logic applies to the bloodsport of recruiting and retaining students. “It’s not a good business strategy to have a name in Idaho that implies you’re a two-year school.” LC State quickly put together a posse. items.body: In 2024 and 2023, contractors and officials with the Idaho State Department of Agriculture treated the Snake River with a copper-based chemical called Natrix to kill quagga mussels. (File photo courtesy of the Idaho State Department of Agriculture) Idaho state officials say they are continuing to push for full eradication of quagga mussels after again detecting the invasive species in the Snake River near Twin Falls earlier this month. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Although quagga mussels and larvae are small, state officials and conservationists say they cause giant problems because of how rapidly they reproduce. A mussel infestation can clog pipes used for irrigation and drinking water, which could have serious effects on the state’s economy, agriculture and recreation industries, officials said. “Our outlook is that not treating this infestation is not an option,” said Sydney Kennedy, a public information officer for the Idaho State Department of Agriculture said in an interview Wednesday. Gov. Brad Little agrees. Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little gives his State of the State Address from the House chambers on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “Other states have shown us what happens when invasive mussel infestations are allowed to establish before action is taken,” Little said in a written statement. “Those delayed responses have resulted in significant long-term management costs coming directly out of taxpayer pockets. Idaho has set the standard by responding aggressively. Our responsible strategy on the Snake River is proving to be effective, and we will continue making decisions that give us the best opportunity to eliminate quagga mussels to protect Idaho’s waters and the people who depend on them.” More than 1,700 different users, including municipal drinking water systems, depend on water from the Snake River, according to the state. Officials at the nonprofit Idaho Conservation League call the detection and presence of quagga mussels a no-win situation and one of the primary threats to the health of the Snake River. This month’s detection marks four consecutive years of finding quagga mussels in the Snake River near Twin Falls. In September 2023, state officials announced for the first time they had detected invasive quagga mussel larvae in water samples . Since 2023, the portion of the river where quagga mussels have been detected has shrunk, the Idaho State Department of Agriculture said. Fewer quagga mussels detected so far this year in Snake River State officials say the number of quagga mussels detected this year is down by 77% compared to last year. As of Aug. 14, the Idaho State Department of Agriculture has detected eight quagga mussel larvae, which are known as veligers, and seven adult quagga mussels. “We know what is at stake if invasive mussels gain a foothold in Idaho,” Idaho State Department of Agriculture Director Chanel Tewalt said in a written statement. “Our previous treatments have proven to be effective, and this level of containment is unprecedented among known quagga mussel infestations. items.body: U.S. District Judge B. Lynn Winmill ruled earlier this month that the state of Idaho cannot regulate abortion when a pregnancy threatens a person’s physical or mental health. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador appealed the decision, and the judge narrowed the ruling to only apply to the Boise doctor that challenged the law. (Otto Kitsinger for the Idaho Capital Sun) An Idaho federal judge has narrowed a previous ruling that had allowed abortions to protect a mother’s health or from self-harm to only apply to the Boise doctor who challenged the law. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador participates in a May 2026 roundtable at the Eisenhower Executive Office Building in Washington, D.C. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Attorney General’s Office) The narrowed ruling issued Tuesday means that Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador and the Ada County prosecutor may not enforce Idaho’s felony abortion ban in cases where Dr. Stacy Seyb administered the procedure because of serious risk of harm due to physical health or mental health concerns. Other doctors in Idaho will still be subject to Idaho’s near-total ban, which includes an exception to prevent the death of the mother but does not include exceptions to prevent her death from self-harm. Elective abortions are completely banned in Idaho. U.S. District Court of Idaho Judge B. Lynn Winmill narrowed the ruling at the request of Labrador, who argued in a recent motion that Winmill’s initial decision was too broad. Winmill agreed with Labrador, citing recent U.S. Supreme Court cases that ruled federal judges in most situations cannot issue “universal injunctions,” which block laws nationwide or more broadly than against the plaintiffs in the case. Winmill wrote “an injunction limited to Dr. Seyb will suffice to address the alleged harm.” Seyb was represented by attorneys from the Lawyering Project and Legal Voice in the case. “While we are disappointed in the ruling, it is only one step in the litigation,” Tanya Pellegrini, co-director of litigation at the Lawyering Project said in an emailed statement. “We will continue to stand with providers and their patients to ensure it is safe to be pregnant in Idaho.” Seyb is a maternal-fetal medicine physician who specializes in high-risk pregnancies. He challenged Idaho’s laws, testifying in court that he’s sent patients out of state amid health concerns because he did not feel comfortable providing abortions under the limited exceptions in Idaho’s law. Idaho’s criminal abortion ban allows an abortion to prevent the death of the mother, to treat ectopic or molar pregnancies, and in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester, if there’s been a police report filed. Doctors who provide abortions that don’t fall within those exceptions face two to five years in prison and revocation of their medical license. The judge denied Labrador’s request to fully eliminate the block on enforcement. Winmill remained “persuaded” abortions to protect women against serious health risks or against death from self-harm were constitutionally protected. Labrador on Aug. 20 also appealed Winmill’s decision to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, arguing the block defies the U.S. Supreme Court decision Dobbs v. The student-led, pro-democracy organization BABE VOTE organized the event. Election Day is Tuesday, Sept. 1. Both Hawes and Naylor are experienced attorneys with different areas of expertise. Hawes has focused on real estate and facilities as in-house corporate counsel. He works for J.R. Simplot Company and was a Boise trustee from 2021 to 2023. Naylor has experience prosecuting child protection cases and was chairman of the Governor’s Task Force on Children at Risk from 2001 to 2016. As enrollment declines, Hawes said the district needs to see facilities as assets. If the district considers closing a school, he would find creative ways to use the building to support the community. “Are there other uses that we can use for facilities that would fit squarely with what the community wants in serving students?” Hawes said. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Around mid-day on a recent Tuesday in Twin Falls, a small plane landed on the tarmac at the Magic Valley Regional Airport but never taxied to the terminal. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Outside the fence surrounding the airport runway area, a group of five people watched through telescopes and binoculars as three white vans drove onto the tarmac. Around 20 men got out of the vans and boarded the plane as law enforcement oversaw the process, which took just over 30 minutes. One man was escorted back off the plane and into a van. According to a flight tracker, the plane then traveled to King County International Airport, or Boeing Field, which is located south of Seattle. Similar flights, operated by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, happen every Tuesday and Thursday at the Magic Valley airport. Shelly McDaniel and her husband Tim McDaniel record the entire boarding process for each ICE flight that operates out of the airport near Twin Falls. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Shelly McDaniel and her husband Tim McDaniel, who live about 30 minutes outside of Twin Falls, have watched every flight since they became involved in efforts to observe them on May 12. The McDaniels have recorded more than 500 detainees being flown out of the airport since flights began in early April. An ICE spokesperson told the Idaho Capital Sun the air operations provide “a network of air transportation to Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) 25 field offices to facilitate the movement of illegal aliens within the United States and their removal to destinations worldwide via air charter and commercial charter services.” “ICE is committed to the safety and welfare of those in custody throughout the entire transfer and removal process,” the spokesperson, who did not provide a name, said in an email. The spokesperson said in the Aug. 12 email that the agency had conducted 20 missions at the Magic Valley airport, also called Joslin Field. The agency’s Salt Lake City Field Office, which oversees Idaho, requests the flights “to support their operations which include the Magic Valley Region.” The Human Rights First ICE flight monitor has recorded 33 flights out of Twin Falls in 2026, and three flights out of the Boise airport. No other Idaho cities are listed. The federal immigration agency has a $1.8 billion contract with CSI Aviation, a private charter and cargo air transportation company, to operate the flights nationwide, according to federal spending data. Airport Manager Matt Barnes told the Sun in an email that the local airport does not have any formal agreement with ICE or CSI Aviation. “We are a public use airport that accepts federal grant funds, so we may not discriminate against aircraft operators who can safely operate at our facility,” Barnes said. ‘I think it’s wrong’; observers watch ICE flights because of due process concerns. She got involved in watching the ICE flights through a local chapter of the group Indivisible, a progressive advocacy organization. “I think it’s wrong,” Stroder said of the flights. “I don’t think people are getting due process. items.body: Middleton School District trustees approved a name and tabled construction bids for the new elementary school at a special Tuesday afternoon meeting. The board tabled voting on a bid package for the new elementary school’s construction because potential bidders were not able to prepare bids in time. It will meet again next week to vote. The new Freedom Elementary, a name voted on by district constituents, won’t be far — in nomenclature or distance — from Independence Elementary, a new elementary school on the West Ada School District side of Star. Middleton’s new elementary will be located on the Canyon County side of Star, a city in two counties. It will serve one of the state’s fastest-growing areas and alleviate overcrowding in two elementary schools. In other action, trustees approved language for a $3 million supplemental levy, spread over two years, to fund teaching and classified positions, new curriculum, school resource officers, classroom technology and a “hot topic:” extracurricular transportation. The deadline for districts to submit ballot language is Friday, Aug. 28. After a failed supplemental levy in May, Middleton administrators made a round of cuts to staff, curricula and logistics. Constituents have been particularly frustrated by the lack of busing for extracurricular activities like sports, trustees said. Superintendent Marc Gee also presented language for a $2.8 million levy, an increase of about $2 per year per $100,000 of property value to taxpayers, over the $3 million option. Trustees didn’t like it. “I would say two dollars makes a big difference when it comes to taking care of our schools that we’re jamming full,” Dempsey said in favor of running the larger $3 million levy. Trustee Jay Clark suggested putting the transportation issue front-and-center in the levy. “That should give us some more votes, if that’s a hot topic,” Clark said. Trustees also approved a list of potential mascots for the new school: Elementary students will vote to choose between being Eagles, Falcons, Pioneers, Patriots or Stars. The board has not yet scheduled a special meeting for next week when it will decide on a bid package for Freedom Elementary’s construction. State law enforcement officials broke ground Tuesday on a new forensics laboratory that they hope will improve the state’s already-fast processing of criminal forensics evidence. And they hope that the $29 million forensics laboratory , based at Idaho State Police’s Headquarters in Meridian, will streamline lab services that are tapped by local and county law enforcement agencies across the state. Moments before officials ceremonially lifted dirt with shovels, Gov. Brad Little talked about the need for the facility in a state that has grown at a record pace in recent years. “The people that have been here expect a safe environment. And you can’t have effective law enforcement if you don’t have the tools that they need to do their job,” Little said. Officials expect construction on the lab to finish in January 2028. The new facility will help aid DNA testing, including advancements to establish Whole Genome Sequencing; examining latent prints; forensics for digital devices; and house technology to help solve gun-related crimes through the National Integrated Ballistic Information Network, officials say. Idaho State Police’s director, Col. Bill Gardiner, praised the agency’s forensics unit as world-renowned and says the laboratory’s construction shows the state’s investment in public safety. “It really is a reflection of those victims and them seeking justice, and those victims seeking closure,” he said before the groundbreaking ceremony. “And that’s really what this lab is there to do: provide that evidence in order to accomplish that.” Right now, Idaho State Police have an average turnaround time for DNA tests of around 30 to 45 days, said Matthew Gamette, the agency’s laboratory system director. While he said that’s already good, law enforcement hopes to routinely provide results within a matter of hours. He praised the agency’s laboratory as efficient already. But he said it’s at its limit. “We have no more space to put scientists in a desk to work. And we have no space to be able to give them analytical space to spread out the evidence and do the analysis. And we have no place to put instruments,” he said in an interview. items.body: Firefighters on the Claremont Fire in Boise, Idaho on July 6, 2026. Drought across the Northwest has exacerbated wildfire conditions in the region. (Photo by Brenen Helgerson/ National Interagency Fire Center) The last weeks of summer find Oregon and much of the Northwest experiencing historic drought, exacerbating what has become one of the most active wildfire seasons in the state and region, according to state and federal climatologists and hydrologists. Beyond fish and ecological impacts, drought across Oregon, Idaho and Washington is causing water supply shortages for public water and electric utilities, costing farmers tens of millions of dollars in lost crops and leaving vegetation and soils dry and susceptible to fires. Wildfire and drought maps overlaid by Oregon’s State Climatologist Larry O’Neill on Monday during an online drought and climate outlook meeting hosted by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration show the summer’s wildfires popping up over historically dry areas of the state and region. About 4% of Oregon’s total land area — 2.4 million acres of mostly rangeland — has burned in the current fire season, most of which occurred within a one-month period. Overall, about 3.5 million acres have burned across the Northwest, including fires in and around Spokane that became some of the most destructive in Washington history. “Drought didn’t cause these ignitions, but they created the conditions with exceptionally dry vegetation and fuels that favor rapid fire growth and extreme impacts once those fires started,” O’Neill said. He and Catherine Fitzpatrick, a hydrologist at NOAA’s Northwest River Forecast Center, detailed water levels and conditions in the Northwest’s rivers, reservoirs and snowpack for a 90-day period, as well as the impacts of temperature anomalies. Even with a potential deluge of precipitation this winter in what O’Neill expects to be a “very strong” or “super” El Niño weather pattern, water reservoirs in the region are so depleted that there’s unlikely to be much carryover in water supplies into next year, the two warned. “Across the Pacific Northwest we’re substantially depleting our reservoir storage, and now we’re getting into kind of the later part of August and September, and reservoirs are being emptied out,” O’Neill said. “There’s little hope for carryover into the next water year, and then as I mentioned earlier, we’re seeing record low stream flows occurring in all three states.” Anomalous heat Most of eastern Oregon and southern Idaho have experienced summer temperatures 2 to 4 degrees Fahrenheit above normal, following what was the warmest fall and winter on record for the entire region, where temperatures in Oregon and Idaho were 3 to 5 degrees Fahrenheit above normal. Most of Oregon east of the Cascades has in the last 90 days experienced “extreme drought,” a NOAA designation indicating major crop and pasture losses, and widespread water shortages or restrictions. About 4% of Oregon in and around Grant, Baker and Wheeler counties in the eastern part of the state are in what NOAA classifies as “exceptional drought,” meaning it reached historic levels, among other indicators. It’s the second time since 2000 that Grant County has received the designation. Despite being surrounded by the Blue Mountains, the area saw the lowest snowpack on record this winter. About 8% of Idaho is experiencing exceptional drought, particularly in Owyhee, Twin Falls and Cassia counties in southern Idaho. Cuts to irrigation water supply for Idaho farmers have cost them $20 million so far according to crop insurance indemnities that are being paid out, O’Neill said, but the total cost is likely to be far higher as many claims won’t be processed until after the growing season ends. In the Yakima Basin in Washington, water users are receiving about 58% of their allotment. That includes the Roza Irrigation district, which supports more than $1.5 billion in annual agricultural revenue for the state.

This month, taxpayers in Texas found out how many students receiving $1 billion in private education subsidies were already homeschooled or enrolled in a private school: 70%. Taxpayers in Idaho are still waiting to get that number from a similar private school choice program that serves nearly nine and a half times fewer students, costs $950 million less and was enacted two months earlier. And it’s not for lack of trying. Between February and July, the Idaho State Tax Commission received seven public records requests related to the Parental Choice Tax Credit. A college faculty member, a hobbyist data analyst, a homeschool advocate, a former public school superintendent and two journalists filed requests seeking data that would shed light on who’s benefitting from the $50 million-a-year taxpayer-funded program. Four of those requests — including two from Idaho Education News — sought the number of tax-credit recipients who previously attended a public school. This data would test a selling point of the program: that it helps students who couldn’t otherwise afford a private education. That tally doesn’t include unofficial requests. Democratic lawmakers, who asked for data in March, weren’t included in a tracking sheet of records requests obtained by EdNews. Nearly all of the requests were denied. items.body: Absentee ballots are prepared to be mailed at the Wake County Board of Elections on September 17, 2024 in Raleigh, North Carolina. (Photo by Allison Joyce/Getty Images) WASHINGTON — With just over two months until the November midterms, the U.S. Supreme Court gave way Monday for President Donald Trump to have a hand in regulating mail-in ballots nationwide, a voting method he has falsely claimed is rife with corruption since he lost the 2020 presidential election. In an unsigned emergency docket opinion , the court’s conservative majority wrote the Trump administration is likely to prevail on its argument that 23 Democratic-led states do not have standing to stop his executive order to change how the U.S. Postal Service processes mail-in ballots. The majority justices also wrote that a lower court’s injunction is “causing irreparable harm,” but left open the possibility that the executive order could still be considered unconstitutional. “The Court’s disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell,” the majority wrote. The legality of a Massachusetts federal district court order, which paused the executive order to overhaul vote-by-mail systems before the Nov. 3 midterms, will now be decided by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit. Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented. In a lengthy dissent, Jackson wrote the ruling “needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections.” The principle of courts not altering voting systems too close to the election has been eroded, she said, amounting to a “Kafkaesque nightmare.” “States administering elections and the voting public that relies on them to do so deserve clarity, not caginess or confusion,” she wrote. Final rule issued The March 31 executive order at the heart of the case in part directs USPS to direct the redesign of mail-in ballot envelopes, including adding a unique barcode. It also asks USPS to collect voters’ names and addresses from state elections officials and directs the U.S. Justice Department to investigate and prosecute state officials who violate the order. The Postal Service issued a final rule Friday detailing how the process would be carried out. Whether an overhaul of mail-in ballots for each state could be completed in time for the Nov. 3 election remains to be seen, as vote-by-mail documents are sent to voters well in advance of Election Day. A federal district judge in Massachusetts chastised the Trump administration for sowing confusion and “creating” an emergency by noticing a rule Friday that the U.S. Postal Service will eventually require federally regulated mail-in ballot voting envelopes and state data. A 95-page notice alerting that the final rule would appear in the Federal Register on Aug. 26 outlined justifications for federal requirements on states to redesign ballot envelopes and provide a list of recipient names and addresses to USPS. The final rule became effective Friday, according to the document. The final rule runs contrary to U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani’s Aug. 11 preliminary injunction barring the federal government from changing states’ mail-in voting rules prior to the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the judge wrote in a brief order on the docket Sunday. “Defendants did not file an appeal and did not seek, let alone obtain, a stay of the preliminary injunction,” Talwani wrote. “Nonetheless, on August 21, 2026, USPS issued its Final Rule, with an anticipated publication date in the Federal Register of August 26, 2026.” Talwani was appointed to the bench by President Barack Obama in 2013 and unanimously confirmed by the Senate the following year. items.body: Idaho Power serves more than 660,000 customers across Idaho and Oregon. The Boise-based utility is looking to sell its Oregon service territory, which represents 4% of its customers, to the Oregon Trail Electric Cooperative for $154 million by early 2027. (Courtesy of Idaho Power) Idaho’s largest utility is seeking a $154 million transfer of all of its Oregon service territory to a locally-owned utility based in Baker City. Idaho Power is awaiting approval from state and federal regulators to sell its Oregon service territory to the Oregon Trail Electric Cooperative, which serves 60,000 customers in John Day, Burns and La Grande across 6,700 square miles. If the sale is approved, the transfer would add 20,000 former Idaho Power customers to the utility’s grid across 4,700 square miles in Malheur, Harney, Baker and Wallowa counties. Idaho Power has served Eastern Oregon customers for more than a century, with those customers representing 4% of the company’s business. Selling its Oregon service territory would allow the company to keep rates affordable for customers as the utility experiences an unprecedented energy demand , according to the company’s application to the Idaho Public Utilities Commission. The sale will not change any of Idaho Power’s customer rates, but new Oregon Trail Electric Cooperative customers will likely see a 5.7% increase to their rates to make up for the cost of the investment, according to the utility. Without the sale, Idaho Power would have needed to raise its general rate for Oregon customers by at least 17% to compensate for the costs of new company investments and inflation. The Oregon Trail Electric Cooperative will buy nearly all of Idaho Power’s distribution lines, substations and equipment located in Oregon. While Idaho Power would no longer serve Oregon retail electric customers, it would continue to own and operate some generation and transmission resources located in Oregon such the Boardman to Hemingway transmission line, which provides power to Idaho, Oregon and across the region. The transfer is expected to close in early 2027.
